passage: Yogesh here, I drive the school van. This morning the teacher told the children to leave their bags at the door, and Dhruv, five, stood frozen. His ears went red. Then he tugged her sleeve. "Miss, I didn't understand. Say it again?" She repeated it slowly and smiled. "Good asking, Dhruv." He nodded and went in. The boy beside him pretended he'd got it and dropped his bag in the wrong spot. I can't say who was more nervous.

qa.q: What is Yogesh's job at the school?
qa.a: He drives the school van.

qa.q: What might Dhruv have felt before he asked the teacher?
qa.a: Some nervousness, hinted by standing frozen with red ears. He could also have been concentrating. He asked anyway.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that made asking easier?
qa.a: She repeated the instruction slowly and praised the asking, so not knowing did not feel shameful.

qa.q: How might the boy who pretended he had understood feel later?
qa.a: Possibly worried or embarrassed once he notices his bag is in the wrong spot, though we cannot be sure what he was thinking.

grounding: Shows a young child saying he did not understand and asking for it again, praised by the teacher, seen by a van driver.

passage: On Monday Parul, six, nodded when her father Harish said, "Put the clothes in the blue box." She put them in the red bag and said nothing. On Wednesday he asked again, and she said quietly, "Papa, which box?" Harish smiled. "Good question. The blue one under the bed." On Saturday at the shop he asked, "Small or big?" Parul said, "I don't understand small. Show me?" He held up both. She pointed, proud.

qa.q: Which box did Harish want the clothes in?
qa.a: The blue one under the bed.

qa.q: What was Parul likely feeling on Monday when she nodded and then used the red bag?
qa.a: Probably unsure and perhaps embarrassed to say so. She may also have been distracted.

qa.q: How can Harish keep encouraging Parul to ask questions?
qa.a: Keep praising the asking, answer patiently, and show things when words are unclear.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when Parul asks, "Papa, which box?"
qa.a: He seems pleased, since he smiled and called it a good question before explaining.

grounding: Shows a child moving from guessing to saying she does not understand, encouraged by a parent.

passage: Construction drilling rattled the classroom windows all morning. Noor Ma'am gave instructions for the craft: “Fold the paper, cut the corner, then glue it on the blue sheet.” Most children started. Divyansh sat still, then raised his hand. “I don't understand. Say it again?” Noor walked over, knelt beside him and said it slowly, one step at a time. Then she said to the class, “Divyansh did a smart thing. He asked instead of guessing.” Divyansh folded his paper, grinning.

qa.q: What was rattling the classroom windows?
qa.a: Construction drilling.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he sat still before raising his hand?
qa.a: He was probably confused and unsure, because he hadn't understood the instructions over the noise.

qa.q: What did Noor Ma'am do that helped other children feel safe to ask?
qa.a: She praised Divyansh in front of the class for asking instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might the other children see asking after Noor's words?
qa.a: They might feel less ashamed about not knowing and more willing to ask themselves.

grounding: In a noisy classroom, a child asks for the instruction again, and the teacher praises asking so no one feels shame.

passage:
“Omkar, go get your jumper, it's cold,” said Joseph.
Omkar ran to his room and came back with his skipping rope.
Joseph laughed, then saw Omkar's face fall. “Not a jumping rope. A jumper, like a sweater.”
Omkar went pink. “I didn't know.”
“That's okay. What could you say next time?”
Omkar thought. “What is a jumper?”
“Exactly. Asking is clever.”
Omkar fetched his sweater, pulled it on, and then asked, “What is a scarf?”
Joseph grinned. “Good question.”

qa.q: What did Omkar bring back instead of a jumper?
qa.a: His skipping rope.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he went pink?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about getting it wrong and a bit hurt when his father laughed.

qa.q: How did Joseph turn the mistake into learning?
qa.a: He noticed Omkar's face, explained the word, and taught him to ask “What is a jumper?” next time, praising asking.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel when Omkar asks about the scarf?
qa.a: He is likely pleased and amused, glad that Omkar feels safe to ask.

grounding: A child guesses wrong about a word, and his father teaches and praises asking for clarification instead.

passage:
“Jagdish, take this to Mrs Rao on the second floor, the flat with the green door, and tell her Amma says thanks.”
Jagdish stood with the box. “Say it again?”
Devika smiled. “Good asking. Second floor. Green door. Mrs Rao.”
“Second floor, green door.” He paused. “What do I say?”
“Amma says thanks.”
“Amma says thanks.” He set off, then came back. “Is the green door left or right?”
“Right. I love that you ask instead of guessing.”
He beamed and ran up the stairs.

qa.q: What colour was Mrs Rao's door?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he asked each question?
qa.a: He was probably unsure but careful, wanting to get the errand right, and felt proud when his mother praised him.

qa.q: Why was praising each question a good idea?
qa.a: It showed Jagdish that asking is good, so he won't feel shame about not knowing.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao see Jagdish arriving with the box?
qa.a: She'd likely be pleased and touched that a small child brought it and passed on the thanks correctly.

grounding: A preschooler asks for directions to be repeated, and his mother praises asking instead of guessing.

passage:
Note from Santosh, paper-craft time, Class KG

I explained how to fold the boat: corners to the middle, then flip, then fold up the edges. Most children began folding.

Pallavi put up her hand. "Say it again. I don't understand the flip part."

I told the class, "Pallavi asked a great question. Asking is a smart thing to do." Then I showed the flip slowly, using her paper.

Three more hands went up after hers. Pallavi's boat was the first one to float in the water tray.

I will keep praising questions like hers.

qa.q: Which part of the folding did Pallavi not understand?
qa.a: The flip part.

qa.q: What was Pallavi likely feeling when she put up her hand?
qa.a: She was probably unsure and a bit confused about the flip, but brave enough to ask instead of guessing. The praise likely left her feeling proud rather than ashamed.

qa.q: Why did praising the question help the whole class?
qa.a: It showed asking is smart, not shameful, so three more children felt safe to ask after Pallavi.

qa.q: How are the three children who raised their hands after Pallavi affected?
qa.a: Pallavi's question and the praise likely made them feel it was safe to admit they were confused too.

grounding: It shows a young child saying "say it again" instead of guessing, and an adult praising the question so she feels no shame about not knowing.
